arguments.name: Resurrection is the decisive truth of Christianity
arguments.conclusion: If Jesus was raised from the dead, Christianity is true, regardless of unresolved secondary disputes.
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
premises: P1: The resurrection is the central, most exciting subject in Scripture.
P2: Denominational and other disputed questions are non-fundamental areas.
P3: Getting the resurrection means 'game, set, and match' for Christianity.
P4: One does not have to solve every problem in the Bible or the world to know the gospel is true.

st1.quote: If Jesus was raised from the dead, Christianity is true.

st2.quote: You don't have to solve every problem in the Bible. We know the most disputed questions in the Bible.

st3.quote: You get the resurrection of Jesus, as my good buddy Mike Licona says, you get the resurrection, it's game, set, and match.

st4.quote: You don't have to solve every big problem in the world, but we do have to know the gospel's true.

st5.quote: A lot of people say, "Christianity is too easy." And other religions, when people die and they do this as if Christians don't, they say, "All you require is for them to believe."

st6.quote: You get the resurrection of Jesus, as my good buddy Mike Licona says, you get the resurrection, it's game, set, and match. Christianity is true.

st8.quote: The resurrection of Jesus is the most exciting, I think, subject in scripture.

arguments.prior_art: Gary Habermas & Mike Licona, The Case for the Resurrection of Jesus, 2004

or1.quote: You get the resurrection of Jesus, as my good buddy Mike Licona says, you get the resurrection, it's game, set, and match.
or1.why: Restates the standard minimal-facts apologetic claim that the resurrection is the linchpin; a variant in rhetorical packaging.

or2.why: No new premise or evidence beyond the standard minimal-facts framing.

arguments.weakest_link: The inference from 'resurrection happened' to 'Christianity is true' is asserted, not argued.
arguments.develop_next: Give an explicit argument that the resurrection entails the truth of Christian doctrine rather than just a miracle.

arguments.name: New Testament belief means trust and surrender, not mere assent
arguments.conclusion: The New Testament word 'believe' means a strong, self-surrendering trust, not merely intellectual agreement.
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
premises: P1: The New Testament was written in Greek, where the word for believe is much stronger than the English word.
P2: Its synonym is trust; it means to jump in with both feet, surrender, and follow.
P3: This is not salvation by works, just as marriage by promise is not marriage by good works.
P4: The marriage vow 'I do' illustrates giving everything one has, which is close to the New Testament meaning of believe.

st1.quote: In the New Testament the word believe means to jump in with both feet.

st2.quote: New Testament, that word is there, believe. Synonym is trust.

st3.quote: But the New Testament's written in Greek, not English. And in the New Testament, the word believe is a very strong word.

st4.quote: We don't call that marriage by good works. We call it marriage by a promise.

st5.quote: You say that that sounds like salvation by works. It's not at all.

st6.quote: That's close. Seriously, that's close to what the New Testament means by believe.

st8.quote: Let me give you an example. We all know, whatever your status in life is, we all know that you can strengthen or ruin uh whatever the rest of your life with two words. I do.

arguments.prior_art: Standard Greek lexicography (pisteuo) as popularized in evangelical preaching; e.g. A. T. Robertson, Word Pictures, 1930s

or1.quote: In the New Testament the word believe means to jump in with both feet.
or1.why: A familiar lexical-theological point with a marriage illustration; variant rather than new argument.

or2.quote: We all know that you can strengthen or ruin uh whatever the rest of your life with two words. I do.
or2.why: The marriage-vow analogy is a fresh illustration, though not new evidence.

arguments.weakest_link: The lexical claim that pisteuo means surrender is asserted from the pulpit without citation of a lexicon or usage data.
arguments.develop_next: Cite specific Greek lexica and NT usage examples distinguishing pisteuo from mere mental assent.

arguments.name: Early creed in 1 Corinthians 15 lists resurrection witnesses
arguments.conclusion: Paul passed on an early creed listing Jesus' death, burial, resurrection, and appearances to Peter, James, the Twelve, all the apostles, the 500, and finally Paul himself.
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
premises: P1: In 1 Corinthians 15:3-5 Paul says he passed on what he received: Christ died for sins, was buried, rose the third day, and appeared.
P2: The list includes two individuals, Peter and James the brother of Jesus, and three groups: the Twelve, all the apostles, and the 500.
P3: Paul adds his own name separately, indicating his appearance was not part of the early creed.

st1.quote: I gave you, I passed on to you the same thing I gave the Corinthians.

st2.quote: And here comes a list to two individuals, Peter and James, the brother of Jesus.

st3.quote: Then Paul adds his own name in verse five. It's added. It's not part of this early creed.

st4.quote: And he said last of all, appeared to me. Three individuals, three groups.

st6.quote: Just says James, but it's brother of Jesus.

st8.quote: In 1 Corinthians 15:3-5 Paul says he passed on what he received

arguments.prior_art: Joachim Jeremias, The Eucharistic Words of Jesus, 1966; Ulrich Wilckens, 1959 (creedal tradition in 1 Cor 15)

or1.quote: I gave you, I passed on to you the same thing I gave the Corinthians.
or1.why: Essentially restates the well-known pre-Pauline creed identification.

or2.why: No new evidence beyond the standard exegesis.

arguments.weakest_link: The claim that verses 3-5 constitute a pre-Pauline creed is asserted rather than demonstrated from linguistic markers.
arguments.develop_next: Show the Aramaic/linguistic indicators that mark the passage as pre-Pauline tradition.

arguments.name: Critical dating still yields early resurrection evidence
arguments.conclusion: Even using skeptical critical dates for the New Testament documents, the evidence for the resurrection remains early and strong.
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
premises: P1: Mark is dated about 70 AD, Luke about 85, John about 90-95, and 1 Thessalonians about 50 AD.
P2: These dates are admitted by critical New Testament specialists, including atheists, agnostics, skeptics, and non-Christian Jews.
P3: Even on their data, one still gets a resurrection.

st1.quote: But I'm I'm trying to show you on their data, you're still going to get a resurrection.

st2.quote: Mark is dated about 70 AD, Luke about 85, John about 90-95, and 1 Thessalonians about 50 AD.

st3.quote: I'm using critical dates. This whole thing, I'm using dates that critics admit.

st4.quote: But I'm I'm trying to show you on their data, you're still going to get a resurrection. That's my point.

st5.quote: A lot of critics say, they jump on the New Testament like they jump on no other ancient book.

st6.quote: Even on their data, one still gets a resurrection.

st8.quote: These dates are admitted by critical New Testament specialists, including atheists, agnostics, skeptics, and non-Christian Jews.

arguments.prior_art: Gary Habermas, 'Evidential Apologetics' and minimal-facts method, 1980s-2000s

or1.quote: I'm using dates that critics admit.
or1.why: The minimal-facts method is Habermas's own, but this is a restatement of it rather than a new argument.

or2.quote: These dates are admitted by critical New Testament specialists, including atheists, agnostics, skeptics, and non-Christian Jews.
or2.why: Uses the concession of critical dating as a dialectical lever, though the dates themselves are standard.

arguments.weakest_link: The step from 'documents are early' to 'therefore the resurrection happened' is a non sequitur without the creedal/eyewitness chain.
arguments.develop_next: Connect the early dates explicitly to the specific creedal content that reports appearances.

arguments.name: Eyewitness memory can reliably span 65 years
arguments.conclusion: The claim that the Gospels are too late because eyewitnesses would have forgotten or died is false; people can reliably recall key events from 65 or more years ago.
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
premises: P1: Critics say that 60 years later nobody remembers such things and all eyewitnesses are dead.
P2: Habermas asks the audience how many clearly recall an eyewitness event from 65 or more years ago, and many hands go up.
P3: It would be wrong to call all those people liars, just as it is wrong to dismiss the Gospel eyewitnesses on that basis.

st1.quote: How many of you clearly recall an event or events from 65 years ago or later, you're sure cuz you were there

st2.quote: It would be wrong to call all those people liars, just as it is wrong to dismiss the Gospel eyewitnesses on that basis.

st3.quote: Folks, there are a lot of hands up right now.

st4.quote: I wouldn't want to call all of them liars, but that's what a lot of people want to say to believers because they think John is way too long at plus 65.

st5.quote: A lot of critics say, they jump on the New Testament like they jump on no other ancient book.

st8.quote: How many of you can remember something you were an eyewitness from 65 or more years ago?

arguments.prior_art: Psychological literature on flashbulb memory (Brown & Kulik, 1977); apologetic use in Habermas, 2000s

or1.quote: How many of you clearly recall an event or events from 65 years ago or later
or1.why: Audience-poll variant of the standard memory argument.

or2.quote: Folks, there are a lot of hands up right now.
or2.why: Uses live audience response as ad hoc data, which the prior literature does not.

or3.why: No cross-domain connection beyond a general appeal to memory.

arguments.weakest_link: A show of hands is anecdotal, self-selected and unverifiable, and does not establish memory reliability for the specific Gospel traditions.
arguments.develop_next: Cite controlled psychological studies on long-term memory for public events and address memory distortion research.

arguments.name: Ancient historical sources are far later than the Gospels
arguments.conclusion: The Gospels and Paul are far better sourced chronologically than standard ancient figures like Alexander the Great and Buddha, so dismissing them as too late is inconsistent.
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
premises: P1: The earliest source for Alexander the Great is almost 300 years after his death, and the two best sources, Arrian and Plutarch, are 425 and 450 years later.
P2: Buddhist Scriptures date from 600 to 800 years after Buddha's death, and a Buddhist PhD author admits Christians have earlier words of their Lord and disciples.
P3: By contrast, Mark is about 40 years after Jesus and Paul's first epistle about 20 years after.
P4: If Alexander and Buddha are accepted as well documented, the Gospels cannot be rejected merely for being 40-65 years later.

st1.quote: We got good information on Alexander. John stinks at plus 60.

st2.quote: The earliest source for Alexander, earliest source, is just short of 300 years later.

st3.quote: The two best sources for Alexander, Arrian and Plutarch, 425 and 450.

st4.quote: If Alexander and Buddha are accepted as well documented, the Gospels cannot be rejected merely for being 40-65 years later.

st5.quote: And critics will say, "That's because the Christians don't write history." Okay, great.

st8.quote: The two best sources for Alexander, Arrian and Plutarch, 425 and 450.

arguments.prior_art: Craig Blomberg / Colin Hemer style comparative ancient-source arguments; popularized in Habermas & Licona, 2004

or1.quote: The earliest source for Alexander, earliest source, is just short of 300 years later.
or1.why: Standard comparative-source apologetic; variant with the Buddha example added.

or2.quote: The sources in this book that I'm bringing to you may be the best sources in Buddhism, with almost any without almost any exception, date from 600 to 800 years after Buddha's death.
or2.why: Adds the Buddhist Scriptures comparison, less common in the prior art.

arguments.weakest_link: Chronological proximity alone does not establish reliability; the argument compares dates, not genre or transmission quality.
arguments.develop_next: Compare transmission methods and genre controls, not just the number of years between events and sources.
